Yes. The papers show two kinds of "lithium-free" cathode: materials that hold no lithium until the cell runs, and whole battery chemistries that use no lithium at all.

## 1. Cathodes that contain no lithium but still work in lithium batteries
Some cathode host materials contain no lithium in their pristine state. The lithium comes from elsewhere in the cell and moves in during discharge.
- **Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅):** It takes up lithium between its layers via V₂O₅ + xLi⁺ + xe⁻ ↔ LiₓV₂O₅ (acsnano-7b02404, p. 4). It is described as a well-studied battery cathode material (p. 2).
- **TiS₂:** It was the positive electrode in the earliest lithium-based battery (ensm-2021, p. 1).
- **Sulfur (in Li–S batteries):** It offers a two-electron transfer per sulfur atom and about 6× the energy density of Li-ion. It also avoids the cost and safety issues of cobalt-containing cathodes. However, anode stability and high areal loadings remain challenges (nanolett-6b05172, p. 1).

## 2. Batteries with no lithium at all (sodium-based)
Two papers demonstrate cathodes in sodium batteries.

**Room-temperature sodium–sulfur battery (nanolett-6b05172)**
- The cathode is sulfur held in microporous carbon made from table sugar, at 35 wt% sulfur (p. 3).
- It delivers over 700 mAh/g of sulfur at 0.1C and 370 mAh/g at 1C (p. 1).
- It keeps over 300 mAh/g across 1,500 cycles at 1C, with Coulombic efficiency above 98% (p. 1).
- Energy density is about 180 Wh/kg, counting the whole electrode mass and an ideal sodium anode (p. 5).
- Challenges compared with lithium–sulfur:
  - much larger volume expansion: 260% for Na versus 80% for Li (p. 2)
  - historically low Coulombic efficiency (p. 2)

**Anode-free sodium battery with a pyrite (FeS₂) cathode (nanolett-6b05174)**
- Pyrite is cheap and abundant but contains no sodium. It therefore had to be "presodiated" before the cell was assembled (p. 5).
- The cell reaches about 400 Wh/kg, based on the mass of the presodiated pyrite and the carbon nucleation layer (p. 5). The authors note this exceeds previous sodium-ion reports. Assuming a 50% packaging penalty, they say it also exceeds current Li-ion technology (pp. 1, 5).
- Stability was shown only over about 40 cycles (p. 4, Fig. 4). The authors say the cathode needs further optimization for cycling stability and rate capability (p. 5).
- Sodium is about 1000× more naturally abundant than lithium (p. 1).

**Other mentions**
- A fully recyclable sodium-ion battery using a Na₃V₂(PO₄)₃ cathode is cited (mattod-2020, p. 9).
- Other papers suggest extending strain engineering to sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium ions (acsnano-7b02404, p. 6).

## Caveat
Most of the other papers here (adma-2020, aenm-2022, ensm-2020) are about **cobalt-free** cathodes, not lithium-free ones. An example is LiNi₀.₈Fe₀.₁Al₀.₁O₂, which still contains lithium. If cobalt-free was what you meant, those papers address it directly.
